chapter_theme: Paripadal 6, the Vaiyai in flood: rain fills the river, the town goes down to water-play, and a husband's quarrel with his wife over the women of the water is settled at the festival.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit hails the river's arrival as a blessing, a praise poem under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the swelling flood that spreads over the land

comparisons.vehicle: புலவர் புகழ் புல நாவின் புனைந்த நன் கவிதை
comparisons.tenor: the flood spreading on without break

paripadal:6:1-13.reading: The sky, having drawn water from the full sea, pours down to set its burden at rest; the flood rises as if to hide the land, the hill herds are troubled and the peacocks call, falls wash the mountain clean, and the cool water runs down the slopes and spreads fast and without pause, like the praise faultless poets keep weaving, so that the work of the fields thrives; and the Vaiyai's coming, met with incense, flowers, oblations and fire, is fit to bring smiling lovers together in their festival finery.
paripadal:6:1-13.nuance: The song opens on the whole water cycle, sea to cloud to hill to river, and ends the sentence not on the harvest but on worship and on lovers dressed for the day (நாளணி): the river's use, for this poet, is the festival. The poets' unceasing verse is the river's measure, so the song names its own craft inside its first image.

thinai_evidence.note: the flood is pictured through lovers' embrace, the union of the river town

comparisons.tenor: the Vaiyai breaking its mountain-built dam

paripadal:6:14-25.reading: As lovers of one desire, in an embrace that tightens bangles, shifts armlets, knots the girdle, muddies the pearl strings, smears the lac of nails and cheeks, turns breast paste to silt and mingles every ornament of breast and chest, break through the restraint that fills the heart, so the Vaiyai broke the dam of its hills; the drum of proclamation sounded, crying that the river's waves had broken the bank, and the whole town roared.
paripadal:6:14-25.nuance: The simile runs the usual way backwards: seven lines of disordered ornaments come before we learn that the subject is a river; the reader first takes it for a love scene. நிறை (the heart's self-restraint) and சிறை (the dam) are set side by side, so the bank that breaks and the reserve that breaks are one word-play. Line 14 is not verse but a modern prose heading left in the text; it is marked here only because the unit must cover it.

thinai_evidence.note: the town at water-play in the river's fords, the play of the riverside land

comparisons.tenor: the rows of cow elephants going down into the water
the water-play of the young, fought as a battle

paripadal:6:26-43.reading: On that day the cow elephants go down in rows, arrayed for water as the spotted-faced tusker is arrayed for war, and the young and the lovers, in fine dress and in wet dress, practise their rivalry in the play of the settling flood as if in battle: with garlands and gear they go down after the rushing current, on elephants' necks and spirited horses, with syringes and horns of scented water, on white pith floats and raft-chariots, the strong playing ford after ford and the well-off at the new water, until the river comes on smelling of juice, mud, ghee and flowers.
paripadal:6:26-43.nuance: The festival is staged as a war (போர் அணி, இகல், அணி அணி ஆகிய தாரர்), with mounts, weapons and ranks, so the puram muster is borrowed for a love game. Lines 37 to 39 (சாரிகை மறுத்து ... சேரி இளையர்) are hard to construe and the reading of them is loose.

thinai_evidence.note: the flood running through the town by night, read through lovers' union

comparisons.tenor: the hill of the flower-garlanded god
the flood that struck the town by night

paripadal:6:44-60.reading: Seeing the river come on reeking, the brahmins bent on their learning are dismayed, take it for a changed flood thick with fragrant clay, and cry that its goodness is gone, for flowers, garlands and wreaths, roots and stalks, fruits and tubers, the food of common people and spilled filtered toddy crowd its water; while the falls that break the hills are praised and the bank-breaking channels cheered, the flood goes down telling the unmated that the god's hill is like the rest between the breasts of lovers met by night, runs through the town, and at faint dawn the cool water of Tamil Vaiyai opens out on the land and shows plainly all that its water-army did in the dark.
paripadal:6:44-60.nuance: The poet sets two judgments of one flood side by side without settling them: for the brahmins the festival water is defiled, for the town it is the season's joy, and the unit closes by calling it தமிழ் வையை, a river owned by the language. The night raid made visible at dawn is the lovers' night told as a river's: the flood's 'army' is the town's lovemaking. Lines 52 and 53 (வாதாலாட்ட, கால் பாராட்ட) are hard to fix, and the speakers of the two quoted cries are not named.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's quarrel with a husband she suspects of another woman, the marutham uri

paripadal:6:61-79.reading: The wife mocks her husband for the wilted shoots he brings, plucked for endless new guests, and asks whether the woman who wore them till his garland faded will not tell what he did with the leaf-skirt in his hand; he answers that the shoots drooped in the water and swears by the red god's hill that the Vaiyai's flood is to blame, and she agrees in scorn: does love keep one nature, now shrinking, now swelling, like the Vaiyai's flood in the rains and in early summer? Keep your Vaiyai, she says, under your own control.
paripadal:6:61-79.nuance: The husband's alibi and the wife's retort use the same river: he blames the flood for the leaves, she turns the flood's rise and fall into the very proof of his changing love. நின் வையை வயமாக வை (line 79) is a gibe: 'your' Vaiyai, the excuse he keeps to hand. The speakers alternate without being named; lines 63 and 64 and 76 are obscure in our text, and line 68 is a modern prose heading, not verse.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's burning reproach of a husband taken by other women

comparisons.vehicle: செல் யாற்றுத் தீம் புனலில் செல் மரம்
comparisons.tenor: the husband's chest, ridden by women who seize men

comparisons.vehicle: வையை உடைந்த மடை அடைத்தக்கண்ணும் பின்னும் மலிரும் பிசிர்
comparisons.tenor: her pain that still burns after he has come back

paripadal:6:80-87.reading: The wife tells him that his chest, like a log drifting down the sweet flowing river, became a raft for women skilled at seizing, that he spent the night away, and that even now, like the spray that keeps welling after the breached sluice of the Vaiyai has been closed, he burns her: though he comes to put out her grief, his coming only keeps scorching the hearts of those whose eyes run with tears.
paripadal:6:80-87.nuance: The images are taken from the day's own water-play: the floats and rafts of the festival become the husband, ridden by others. The dammed sluice that still seeps answers the reconciliation he expects: his return closes the breach, but the hurt goes on leaking. Line 82 (என்னும் பனியாய் இரவெல்லாம் வைகினை) is uncertain in its first words.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife questions the crushed garland, the husband defends himself

paripadal:6:88-96.reading: The husband explains that while she stood on the bank a woman bathing in his pool, swept under by a wave, came up and fell on him unawares, and that before he could take hold of her she was up again; the wife asks who it was that pressed into his garland and what touched it, he tells her to understand that there is no other river but this Vaiyai to blame, and when she scorns the answer he swears with his hand on his head by cool Parankunram.
paripadal:6:88-96.nuance: The festival gives the husband a ready alibi, since everyone is in the water together and bodies do collide; the poem lets the excuse be plausible and the suspicion be reasonable at once. The oath is by the god's hill above the river, the same Murugan shrine the Akananuru husbands swear by. Who speaks lines 92 to 96 is not marked in the text; the split given here is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the sulk is ended by counsel and pleading, the close of marutham oodal

comparisons.tenor: love that spreads in the players' hearts

paripadal:6:97-107.reading: Others urge the wife: do not be angry; he fears the reddening of your eyes, so leave the sulk and begin the play, for a sulk that festers too long spoils love, and to burn and drive off into the dark night a heart that is yours alone would be the fault; and so, while the household plays and the skilled plead and labour until the sulk is understood, the lovers revel and bathe, grant grace and sulk again here and there as love puts out its tendrils, and the poet asks the Vaiyai that the love which has bloomed in the players' hearts may never fade.
paripadal:6:97-107.nuance: The quarrel of the dialogue is not left to the two lovers: the town's skilled appeasers (வல்லவர்) do the work of reconciliation, and sulking is named as part of the play (அளிப்ப, துனிப்ப), not its interruption. The closing prayer turns the river from cause of the quarrel into keeper of the love. The counselors of lines 97 to 101 are not named; `pira` stands for them. The word கொடி for love's spreading is figurative, so it is not listed as karu.

links.note: Kural 18 says that if the sky dries, festival and worship cease even for the gods; Paripadal 6.1-13 shows the rain that has come ending in incense, flowers, oblation and fire (புகை, பூ, அவி ஆராதனை, அழல்) at the river's arrival.
links.teaches: The Kural argues from absence that worship hangs on rain, and the Paripadal shows the positive side as one continuous scene from sea to cloud to river to offering, adding what the couplet leaves out: the same flood that feeds the rite also brings lovers together, so festival here means love as much as worship.

links.note: Kural 1251 has desire's axe break the door of restraint (நிறை); Paripadal 6.22-23 has the flood break its dam as lovers of one desire break the restraint that fills the heart (உளம் நிறை உடைத்தென).
links.teaches: The Kural's woman speaks of restraint broken as her private defeat, while the Paripadal makes the same breaking of நிறை the measure of a flood the whole town celebrates with drums, so the pair shows the Kural's image of a lost guard was also, in the festival, a public and welcome release.

links.note: Akananuru 296 makes the husband's bathing in the great Vaigai with a dark girl the gossip of Koodal; Paripadal 6.26-43 shows the whole town, young and old, rich and strong, going down to play in the same river.
links.teaches: Read against the Paripadal's crowd at the fords, the Akananuru friend's charge cannot be that he bathed in the Vaigai, since everyone did; the scandal lies in whom he bathed with, so the akam reproach depends on a public festival that the akam poem itself never describes.

links.note: Naladiyar 370 says fresh floodwater and a courtesan's friendship are alike, both ending when their source ends; Paripadal 6.72-75 has the wife say love's shrinking and swelling is the Vaiyai's flood.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar uses the flood's ebb to condemn bought love and spare the household, but the Paripadal puts the same flood image in the wife's mouth against her own husband, so the didactic contrast of faithful wife and fickle courtesan breaks down once the river festival shows the husband's love rising and falling like the stream.

links.note: Kural 1134 says love's fierce flood carries off the raft (புணை) of shame and manliness; Paripadal 6.80-81 says the husband's chest, like a log in the river, became a raft (புணை) for women skilled at seizing.
links.teaches: In the Kural the raft is the lover's own virtue swept away by his desire, in the Paripadal the man himself is the raft that others ride, so the same river figure moves from an inner confession to a wife's accusation, and the festival's real floats show where the Kural's metaphor came from.

links.note: Naladiyar 222 says those who live by water do not rage when the flood breaks the dam but dam it again, as one bears a valued friend's repeated wrongs; Paripadal 6.83-87 says that even when the breached sluice is closed the spray still wells, as her burning goes on after he returns.
links.teaches: The two poems use the same breached dam for opposite claims: the Naladiyar makes re-damming the picture of calm forbearance that works, while the Paripadal wife says closing the breach does not stop the leak, so the pair shows that the moralist's patience is exactly what the wronged wife declares impossible.

links.note: In Akananuru 266 the wife says the husband's water-play with young women in the evening flood is gossip but that what hurts is his oath by Murugan of Alaivay; in Paripadal 6.88-96 the husband, accused after the water-play, swears by cool Parankunram.
links.teaches: Both husbands answer a water-play charge with an oath to a Murugan shrine, but the Akananuru wife treats the oath as the worse betrayal while the Paripadal lets the oath pass into a reconciliation brokered by others, so the pair shows the festival hymn softening into play what the akam anthology records as a wound.

links.note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that whatever garland he wears she says he wore it for another woman; in Paripadal 6.91-92 the wife asks who pressed into his garland and what touched it, and he blames the river.
links.teaches: The Kural states the suspicious garland as a pure case of love's jealousy, with no cause given, while the Paripadal gives the garland a real crushing and a real crowd in the water, so the pair shows the couplet's general complaint distilled from a festival in which the evidence truly could point either way.

links.note: Kural 1302, spoken by the friend, says sulking is like salt and a little too much spoils it; Paripadal 6.98-99 has those around the wife say that if the sulk festers much love is spoiled (துனி நனி கன்றிடின் காமம் கெடூஉம்).
links.teaches: The same counsel to a sulking wife appears in both, but the Paripadal shows it said aloud at the festival and then acted on by skilled pleaders until the sulk is understood, so the Kural's measure of salt turns out to belong to a social practice of reconciliation, not only to one friend's private advice.

new_concepts.gloss: water-play in the river or pool, especially the festival bathing of the town and of lovers in the new flood
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's words (Paripadal 6, line 30: தணி புனல் ஆடும்)

source_issues: Paripadal 6 line 14 is a modern prose heading left in the verse text (it summarises the bank breaking and the town rising); it is not verse.
Paripadal 6 line 68 is likewise a modern prose heading (it names the flood as the cause of the wilted shoots), not verse.
Paripadal 6: the core text has 107 lines but the source numbers its last line 106; printed line 15 stands on line 16 (flag), consistent with the heading at line 14 being counted.
Paripadal 6: the builder dropped lines it took for headings at positions 11, 48, 63 and 75 (flags); these could not be checked by eye against a second edition in the corpus.
Paripadal 6 line 63 is not in sangamtamil.com's text (flag); ours kept.
Paripadal 6: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.
